Note::from_windows1252¶

Back to Note API Reference

Signature¶

Note Note::from_windows1252() const

Decode Windows-1252 Bytes Into UTF-8 Text¶

from_windows1252() reads each cell’s bytes as Windows-1252 (the “ANSI” code page long used by Windows and still common in exported CSVs, email, and older web pages) and returns a UTF-8 text-mode Note. It is the natural choice over from_latin1 when the source is Windows software, because Windows-1252 fills the 0x80–0x9F range — which Latin-1 leaves as control codes — with printable characters: the euro sign 0x80 → €, the smart quotes 0x91–0x94 → ‘ ’ “ ”, the dashes 0x96 0x97 → – —, the bullet 0x95 → •, and so on.

Bytes 0x00–0x7F and 0xA0–0xFF decode exactly as in Latin-1. Five positions in the 0x80–0x9F block are unassigned in Windows-1252 (0x81, 0x8D, 0x8F, 0x90, 0x9D); each of those becomes a literal ?. Every other byte maps to exactly one character, so the decode never raises.

The operation is shape-preserving and cell-independent, and the result is tagged UTF-8 text regardless of input mode. The inverse is to_windows1252_lossy.

Example 1: Smart Punctuation And The Euro Sign¶

const pluss::Note raw = pluss::note::bytes(
    {std::string("\x93") + "quote" + "\x94" + " " + "\x97" + " bullet " +
     "\x95" + " euro " + "\x80"});
std::cout << pluss::note::print(raw.from_windows1252()) << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[1], dim=1, numel=1, encoding=utf8)
["“quote” — bullet • euro €"]

Example 2: Unassigned Bytes Become ?¶

std::cout << pluss::note::bytes({std::string("x\x81y\x8d") + "z"})
                 .from_windows1252()
          << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[1], dim=1, numel=1, encoding=utf8)
["x?y?z"]

0x81 and 0x8D have no Windows-1252 character, so each decodes to ?.

See Also¶

  • Note::to_windows1252_lossy: the inverse.

  • Note::from_latin1: the plain ISO-8859-1 decode, without the 0x80–0x9F characters.

  • Note::to_utf8_lossy: use instead when the bytes are already UTF-8.
